extracted.intended_audience: newspaper writers, opinion journalists, and general essayists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and ethical/practical criteria for newspaper/editorial and opinion-essay writing, plus general rules for truthful, fair, and effective public prose. Emphasizes accuracy, restraint, moral courage, and avoidance of fads and sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Print nothing you would not say to a man's face
rubrics_metrics.description: Print nothing of a man which I would not say to his face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical rule for journalism: print nothing in malice; think twice before consigning a suspect to the ruin of printer's ink; respect the old and defend the weak; be fair in personal attacks; generally avoid hidden malice or anonymous villification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vindictiveness in public discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: From first to last throughout the angry debates... not one vindictive, prescriptive word fell from his tongue or pen (referring to Lincoln).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in heated controversy, refrain from vindictive language; seek temperate, humane expression rather than recrimination or prescriptive bitterness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify facts by pursuing original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Where occasion seemed to require, to pursue to original sources in quest of accuracy. In no instance has he found any essential error in his narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to letters, criticisms and challenges by checking primary sources; prioritize factual accuracy and corroboration over hearsay or guesswork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about scope — personal recollection vs. comprehensive history
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes he has been charged with omissions--as if he were writing a history of his own times--whereas he has been only, and he fears, most imperfectly, relating his immediate personal experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the intent and limits of your work; if writing personal recollections, do not present them as exhaustive history; acknowledge omissions and the personal nature of the account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fads and fashionable rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: The League of Nations is a fad. Politics, like society and letters, has its fads... A taking issue is as a stunning gown, or 'a best seller.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of fashionable causes and catchy slogans that 'tickle the ear without convincing the sense.' Favor substance, durable argument and practical consequences over ephemeral vogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer facts and pragmatism over abstract theories
rubrics_metrics.description: I am a jingo myself. But a wicked material jingo, who wants facts, not theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In political and public writing, emphasize concrete realities, costs, and practicalities rather than airy abstractions or idealistic schemes divorced from fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid doctrinaire posturing from an overeducated tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The overeducated mind fancies himself a doctrinaire when he is in point of fact only a disciple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of overrefinement that produces half-baked dogma; temper learned rhetoric with common sense and avoid presenting learned repetition as original conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing requires heart as well as intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: The pen is mightier than the sword only when it has behind it a heart as well as a brain. He who wields it must be brave, upright and steadfast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective prose combines moral courage, integrity and conviction with intellectual skill; rhetorical facility alone is insufficient without ethical backbone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject sentimentality and 'gush' in serious political writing
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing but sentiment--gush and gammon--in the proposed League of Nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sentimental appeals and empty emotionalism in place of reasoned argument; sentiment should not substitute for concrete policy or rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of pandering to 'the people' or mob-appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: From fakers... we hear a great deal about 'the people'... The people en masse constitute what we call the mob. Mobs have rarely been right--never except when capably led.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not uncritically appeal to or pander to vague majoritarian sentiment; recognize the dangers of crowd-thinking and the need for capable leadership and reasoned argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist grand schemes that would standardize or flatten humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Freedom...would standardize it. The effect of that would be to desiccate the human species in human conceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution toward utopian or universal schemes that promise to 'recreate the Universe' or standardize human behavior; value individuality and beware of flattening human variety for ideological ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate events truly and interpret fairly
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us relate them truly and interpret them fairly. If the South would have the North do justice to its heroes, the South must do justice to the heroes of the North.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice balanced historical judgment: give credit where due on all sides, avoid partisan misrepresentation, and aim for fairness in interpretation and narrative.
